claims.text: The AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles are synthesized by pulsed laser deposition on a silicon nitride membrane.
The initial nanoparticles are smaller than 5 nm.
The initial nanoparticles have elliptical or icosahedral geometries.
The nanoparticles initially exhibit a metastable FCC structure.
Au and Cu segregate to the nanoparticle surface during heating.
Surface-segregated Au and Cu subsequently evaporate.
Surface-energy minimization gradients drive Au and Cu segregation rather than configurational entropy suppressing diffusion.
The segregation and evaporation mechanism becomes dominant above approximately 600 K.
Au and Cu are low-surface-energy elements relative to the other constituents and therefore enrich the nanoparticle surface.
Surface compositional gradients create a chemical-potential gradient that drives atomic flux.
The high surface-to-volume ratio of sub-5 nm nanoparticles makes surface-energy minimization the dominant driving force.
Surface-energy minimization lowers the activation-energy barrier for surface diffusion.
The reduced surface-diffusion barrier permits rapid migration of Au and Cu to the surface despite nominally sluggish diffusion.
The lower cohesive energy of surface-enriched Au and Cu causes their preferential evaporation.
Preferential evaporation causes nanoparticle shrinkage and reshaping toward spherical geometries.
Accelerated Au/Cu segregation and evaporation lead to rapid loss of sub-5 nm particles and widening of the particle-size distribution.
Icosahedral particles reshape into spheres faster than truncated-octahedral particles because icosahedra have higher surface strain energy.
The proposed surface-energy-dominated mechanism applies only to nanoparticles smaller than 10 nm.
The proposed mechanism does not apply to bulk alloys or nanoparticles larger than 50 nm, where bulk diffusion kinetics dominate.
